printed_headline_estimate: Ordinal logit on JMP drinking water ladder (N = 535, Table 4, p. 9): Lilongwe urban vs. rural OR = 5.00, 95% CI (2.90, 8.62), p = 0.000 (Pseudo R2 = 0.1041); Binary logit on 24-h water availability (N = 535, Table 8, p. 10): Lilongwe urban OR = 1.487624, SE = 0.339038, p = 0.081; Independent-means t-test on round-trip collection time (Table 5, p. 10): urban 8.74 min (SD = 9.66) vs. rural 19.65 min (SD = 19.49), t = -8.2547, df = 533, p = 0.000; Chi-square tests on main water source chi2(5) = 411.6280, p < 0.001 (Table 2, p. 7) and JMP ladder chi2(3) = 90.8539, p < 0.001 (Table 3, p. 9) — all testing coarse urban-vs.-rural geography and socio-demographics rather than a Criterion 2 legal/institutional exposure.
rationale: Full text (18 pages) read completely. The study surveys N = 535 households in Lilongwe, Malawi (262 in three high-density urban neighborhoods and 273 in villages around two rural trading centers) and reports genuine inferential statistics (chi-square tests in Tables 2-3, multivariate ordinal logistic regression on JMP drinking water ladder in Table 4, independent-samples t-test on collection time in Table 5, and binary logistic regression on 24-hour availability in Table 8). However, every inferential model tests only a coarse geographic indicator (Lilongwe urban vs. Lilongwe rural) alongside household socio-demographic predictors (sex of household head, farming vs. non-farm occupation, literacy, marital status, and monthly income). Affordability (Table 6: 12.36% urban vs. 1.75% rural monthly income spent on water) and perceived livelihood burdens (Table 9) are reported descriptively only (means and SDs). The rule-type legal and institutional mechanisms relevant to Criterion 2—specifically the Waterworks Act of 1995 restricting Water Boards' statutory jurisdiction to urban areas, Lilongwe Water Board's 2020-2025 full-cost recovery tariff policy, and the 62.2% vacancy rate in rural water institutions—are not measured or tested quantitatively and appear solely in an ex-post narrative discussion in Section 4.4 (p. 15) drawing on secondary documents. Because a generic urban-versus-rural geographic dummy confounds urbanization, population density, and physical infrastructure proximity with statutory utility jurisdiction, the tested quantitative exposure fails narrow Criterion 2 and does not yield a SWiM-eligible effect.

rationale: The full text empirically evaluates a narrow Criterion 2 Family C utility ownership/corporatization mechanism—management by Minas Gerais's state water and sanitation company COPASA (partially privatized via a 2006 stock-exchange IPO) versus local municipal/autonomous public service organizations—on Criterion 4 household water and sanitation access outcomes across municipalities in Minas Gerais using IBGE 2000 and 2010 Census data. Specifically, the authors compute 2000-2010 municipal first-differences for municipalities exclusively served throughout the decade by COPASA (n = 64) versus municipal organizations (n = 256, total N = 320) and apply independent-samples Mann-Whitney U tests at 95% reliability (alpha = 0.05). COPASA municipalities exhibited a significantly smaller increase in the percentage of households connected to the general water network (Fig. 3, p < 0.05) and a significantly smaller reduction in households lacking a bathroom/WC (Fig. 6, p < 0.05), while differences in 2000-2010 changes for general sewage/rainwater network connection (Fig. 5) and bathroom/WC presence (Fig. 4) were not statistically significant at the 95% level. Although Tables 2-12 and Figures 1-8 are embedded as raster images in the PDF (requiring visual inspection of the PDF pages to transcribe exact numeric medians/means or exact p-values if printed inside the plots), the prose itself provides directionally interpretable inferential two-group change contrasts, group sample sizes (64 vs. 256), and 95%-confidence significance results directly eligible for Family C SWiM synthesis.

rationale: This mixed-methods cross-sectional study in urban Dhaka combines a quantitative matched survey of N = 384 landlord households (192 connected to DWASA foul-water sewers and 192 connected to storm/open drains on the same lanes) with qualitative KIIs (n = 5 DWASA officials), IDIs (n = 10 landlords), and secondary fee schedules. Although the paper reports inferential bivariate statistics (chi-square, t-tests, Mann-Whitney U, and ANOVA with p-values and Cohen's d in Tables 2-4), none of the tested quantitative pairs link a narrow Criterion 2 rule-type legal, tenure, administrative, tariff, or regulatory exposure to a Criterion 4 WASH access outcome. Specifically: (1) 100% of both groups are resident formal house owners/landlords on sewered streets (zero tenure or service-zone variation); (2) quantitative differences test only socio-demographic/housing-age characteristics (e.g., settlement/building duration since construction, p = 0.008), ex-post monthly water/sewer bills resulting from connection ($27 vs $22, p = 0.0002), hypothetical payment motivators, and individual RANAS psychological/attitudinal constructs (perceived health risk, social status, self-efficacy, injunctive norms, and general subjective beliefs about whether cost, awareness, or 'legal issues' obstruct connection [7.3% vs 8.9%, p = 0.574]); and (3) all evidence on narrow Criterion 2 institutional/administrative mechanisms—lengthy DWASA connection approvals (>2 years), DWASA permit/connection fees ($84-$342 USD) versus city corporation drain fees ($41 USD), police fines for unpermitted road-cutting, historical 1990-2000 fee-free connection waves, and DWASA-city corporation coordination failures—is strictly qualitative/descriptive (pp. 10, 12-16).

rationale: Full text (17 pages) examined. Although described as a mixed-methods forensic disaster study, its quantitative component is strictly descriptive and deterministic rather than inferential. Specifically, the authors report: (1) Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI3, SPI6, SPI12) anomalies from ERA5 rainfall data (1991-2021); (2) descriptive monthly national load-shedding GWh and daily reservoir storage percentages; (3) municipal tanker/borehole counts and audit figures from secondary reports; and (4) a deterministic arithmetic indicator of per-capita water supply (dam storage multiplied by a 47% leakage estimate with a deterministic 30%-60% scenario band, divided by census population, falling from 106 to 15 L/capita/day). Governance, corruption, dual traditional/municipal authority, and emergency tanker failures are analysed qualitatively through 31 semi-structured interviews mapped onto a Pressure-and-Release (PAR) diagram and a qualitative Causal Loop Diagram (CLD). No inferential tests, regressions, correlations, standard errors, confidence intervals, or p-values appear anywhere in the paper.

printed_headline_estimate: Linear regression of village-level latrine coverage in March 2012 (%) across N = 50 intervention villages (based on n = 170 VWSC members and n = 408 households; Table 4, PDF p. 11): >=5 VWSC meetings held since start of programme beta = 0.178 (95% CI: 0.010; 0.346, p = 0.04); village motivator visited house in past month beta = 0.216 (95% CI: -0.000; 0.431, p = 0.05 in Table 4; p = 0.02 in text on PDF p. 7); seen wall paintings (showing F-diagram and latrine cost breakdown) beta = 0.171 (95% CI: 0.001; 0.341, p = 0.05); heard/participated in transect walk/mapping exercise beta = 0.637 (95% CI: -0.104; 1.379, p = 0.09); heard/participated in wealth ranking exercise beta = 1.530 (95% CI: -2.261; 5.321, p = 0.42); heard of VWSC beta = 0.181 (95% CI: -0.660; 0.428, p = 0.15); VWSC members attended NGO training beta = 0.001 (95% CI: -0.181; 0.183, p = 0.99). (BPL vs APL latrine coverage [68% vs 61%, PDF p. 4] and overall intervention latrine coverage [8% baseline to 66% in March 2012, PDF pp. 1, 4] report no inferential tests; Table 2 t-tests [PDF pp. 8-9, n = 807] test awareness outcomes only.)
rationale: This process evaluation of India's Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC) across 100 cluster-randomised villages in Orissa reports three distinct sets of quantitative findings: (1) descriptive-only latrine coverage contrasts for overall intervention progress (8% at baseline to 66% in March 2012, p. 4) and Below Poverty Line vs Above Poverty Line cardholders (68% vs 61%, p. 4, after implementers exercised discretion to extend subsidies to all households to avoid conflict, p. 7), with no SEs, CIs, or p-values; (2) inferential village-level t-tests between intervention and control arms (Table 2, pp. 8-9, n = 807 households) that test campaign/VWSC awareness rather than sanitation access (failing Criterion 4); and (3) inferential village-level linear regressions across the N = 50 intervention villages (Table 4, p. 11; built from n = 408 households and n = 170 Village Water and Sanitation Committee [VWSC] members) testing associations between village-level latrine coverage in March 2012 (Criterion 4 sanitation coverage) and mandated TSC governance, participatory targeting, and outreach/support mechanisms. Specifically, active functioning of the TSC-mandated VWSC (>=5 VWSC meetings held since programme start: beta = 0.178, 95% CI 0.010 to 0.346, p = 0.04) and household outreach visits by village motivators (beta = 0.216, 95% CI -0.000 to 0.431, p = 0.05 in Table 4; p = 0.02 on p. 7) show positive associations with village latrine coverage, alongside non-significant estimates for participatory wealth ranking (used to identify poor non-BPL households for subsidy eligibility; beta = 1.530, p = 0.42), PRA mapping/transect walks (beta = 0.637, p = 0.09), and NGO training of VWSC members (beta = 0.001, p = 0.99). These Table 4 estimates fit SWiM Family B (assistance/participation/external-support, with secondary governance overlap with Family A/C for VWSC institutional activity). Confidence is rated medium because under an ultra-strict reading of narrow Criterion 2 requiring formal legal/rule-status variation rather than variation in de facto VWSC meeting regularity, participatory targeting, and outreach intensity across villages under uniform TSC rules, Table 4 sits near the implementation-fidelity boundary while the strict BPL-card rule contrast (68% vs 61%) is descriptive only.

printed_headline_estimate: Table 4, Model 3 (PDF p. 15 / p. 139, N = 1235, survey-design-adjusted heterogeneous choice ordinal logit with robust SEs): Formal ownership (formal-title dwelling ownership) OR = 1.84, p < 0.001 predicting higher reported household municipal-service coverage deficits (0 = no deficit, 1 = 1-2 service deficits, 2 = 3-4 service deficits across municipal water, sewage, electricity, and solid waste); bivariate association of formal ownership with no deficit is positive (p = 0.00, PDF p. 14 / p. 138), and supplementary Model 3 interaction formal home ownership X log head's years in neighbourhood OR = 1.93, p = 0.00 (Table 4 note a, PDF p. 15; 95% CI for predicted probability of no deficit: 0.01-0.99 vs. 0.14-0.98, Appendix A note b, PDF p. 24). Also in Table 4 Model 3 (N = 1235): Reported household community participation OR = 0.89, p < 0.01; Reported no. community organisations OR = 1.31, p < 0.01. In Table 3 Model 3 (PDF p. 11-12 / p. 135-136, N = 1235): Community or government action established municipal water service predicts formal-title ownership vs. non-ownership with OR = 2.15, p < 0.001 (predicted probability 95% CIs: 0.37-0.40 vs. 0.53-0.61, Appendix A, PDF p. 23).
rationale: Using a stratified probability survey of lower- to middle-income districts in San Salvador (sub-sample N = 1243; regression N = 1235), Tardanico (2008) estimates survey-design-adjusted heterogeneous choice ordinal logit regressions with robust standard errors (Table 4, PDF p. 15 / p. 139) testing a canonical Family A legal/tenure mechanism—formal-title dwelling ownership ('Household owns dwelling with formal title: 1 = yes, 0 = no')—on household municipal-service coverage deficits (0 = no deficit, 1 = 1-2 missing services, 2 = 3-4 missing services across municipal water [9% deficit], sewage [15% deficit], electricity [2% deficit], and solid waste [21% deficit]). Bivariately and with respondent controls only, formal ownership significantly predicts having no municipal service deficit (p = 0.00, PDF p. 14 / p. 138), but in the full model controlling for macro-structural assets (including an index containing indoor toilet) and log head's years in neighbourhood, formal ownership reverses sign to predict higher odds of service deficit (OR = 1.84, p < 0.001), explained by an interaction with log head's years in neighbourhood (OR = 1.93, p = 0.00; formal ownership reduces deficits only among newer neighbourhood residents/newer housing stock). Table 4 Model 3 also reports inferential estimates for household community participation (OR = 0.89, p < 0.01; Family B) and number of community organisations (OR = 1.31, p < 0.01), while social security coverage is positively associated with no deficit bivariately (p = 0.00) and univariately before becoming attenuated by macro controls (p. 138). Note for synthesisers: the municipal-service deficit outcome is a 4-utility composite combining municipal water and sewage with electricity and solid waste rather than a standalone water-only or sanitation-only indicator, and Model 3 adjusts for dwelling physical features (including inside toilet), which reverses the positive bivariate association between formal title and full service coverage.

rationale: Full text read (14 pages, in Spanish). The study combines descriptive tabulation and GIS mapping of the 2009 CESPT residential water account registry (N = 495,684 active residential accounts in Tables 1-2; 346,979 mapped accounts in Map 2) with 34 semi-structured interviews (20 officials, 10 tanker-truck users in irregular settlements in Valle Redondo, 2 tanker operators, and 2 standpipe concessionaires). Substantively, the paper documents a rule-based tenure and tariff-regulation mechanism: CESPT requires legal land tenure for piped network connection, forcing irregular settlements to buy unregulated tanker ('pipa') water at $100/m3 versus $12.18-$12.19/m3 for formal metered users in 2010 (~8x higher, Table 3) and restricting irregular-settlement consumption to ~8 L/person/day versus 47 L/person/day among the lowest 50.63% of formal accounts. However, the empirical analysis is strictly descriptive and qualitative—reporting frequencies, percentages, group means, tariff schedules, and choropleth maps with zero inferential hypothesis tests, regressions, correlation coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals, test statistics, or p-values (uses of 'significativamente' and 'correlación' in the prose are purely colloquial). Flagging quantitative_synthesis_eligible = TRUE is therefore overstated.

rationale: Full text (17 pages) is accessible and reports inferential statistics (one-way ANOVA with post-hoc comparisons, pairwise correlations with Holm adjustment, and a multiple regression summarized from Appendix 2 on N = 965 households across 8 community water supply systems in Cali and Restrepo, Colombia). All 8 studied systems are formal community Water Users' Associations (WUAs), and the inferential analyses test only socio-economic/demographic household characteristics (household size, education, age, occupation) and spatial location/system IDs (peri-urban vs. rural zone defined by distance from Cali) against self-reported perceived indoor water use habits (estimated from self-reported fixture use durations and literature flow rates, assuming shower use even during intermittent supply). Institutional/regulatory attributes such as Water Use Efficiency Program (WUEP) adoption, WUA staffing, and billing are reported only descriptively across the 8 systems in Tables 2-3 without inferential testing. Thus, the study falls under inferential_non_swim_or_out_of_scope.

printed_headline_estimate: Tobit regressions of voluntary 3-month household O&M cash (CASHCONT, ETB) and labour (LABORCONT, days) contributions (N = 160 surveyed households across 16 systems; uncensored N = 140 for cash [chi2 = 72.03, Pseudo R2 = 0.12] and N = 135 for labour [chi2 = 76.22, Pseudo R2 = 0.15]; Table 4, PDF p. 10 / p. 994; marginal effects in Table 5, PDF p. 13 / p. 997; SEs not printed): Participation in project design/implementation (DPARDPIMP): cash beta = 0.45 (p < 0.01), dy/dx = 0.37 ETB/month; labour beta = 0.18 (p < 0.05), dy/dx = 0.13 days/month. Health-promoter advocacy (ADVOCACY): cash beta = 0.12 (ns), dy/dx = 0.10; labour beta = 0.32 (p < 0.01), dy/dx = 0.22 days/month. Trust in WUCs (TOWUCs): cash beta = 0.19 (p < 0.10), dy/dx = 0.16; labour beta = -0.05 (ns), dy/dx = -0.03. Household income (INCOME, per ETB 1,000): cash beta = 0.03 (p < 0.10), dy/dx = 0.03; labour beta = 0.04 (p < 0.01), dy/dx = 0.03. No household or community water access/service outcome is estimated.
rationale: Full text (17 PDF pages) is accessible and reports inferential Tobit regressions (Table 4, p. 994; Table 5, p. 997; N = 160 households across 16 rural water systems in Achefer, Ethiopia). However, the study fails Criterion 4 (and narrow Criterion 2) for SWiM synthesis: the sole dependent variables in the econometric models are households' voluntary cash contributions (CASHCONT, in ETB) and voluntary labour contributions (LABORCONT, in days) over the preceding 3 months toward system protection and maintenance (described by the authors as willingness-to-pay cash and willingness-to-contribute labour). No household or community water supply service access outcome (such as connection, coverage, functionality/reliability, continuity, quantity, water quality, or affordability/exclusion) is analysed as a dependent variable (subjective water satisfaction WASATS and perceived source safety PSOWS enter only as explanatory covariates predicting O&M contributions and are statistically insignificant). Moreover, the main significant predictors (self-rated degree of participation during NGO project design/implementation, health-promoter advocacy, household income, and trust in WUCs) are participatory project-delivery, attitudinal, and socioeconomic factors rather than a rule-type legal/administrative/tariff/tenure exposure tested on service access.

publication_year_note: 2019 PhD dissertation submitted to West Virginia University (Graduate Theses, Dissertations, and Problem Reports, ETD 7424; '2019' and 'Copyright 2019 Fahad Alzahrani' printed on PDF pp. 1-2).
printed_headline_estimate: Essay 1 (Table 2.4, PDF p. 68, Spatial Durbin Model with RE & year FE, N = 576 state-years, DV = log real per capita health care expenditures): SDWA health-based violation exposure direct elasticity = 0.005 (p = 0.008), indirect = 0.035 (p = 0.003), total = 0.040 (p = 0.003). Essay 2 (Sec. 3.6, PDF pp. 97-102, hedonic OLS/SLM/spatial quantile regressions, N = 1,985 home sales in Marion County, WV, DV = ln(property sale price)): OLS BWN coefficients -0.0065 to -0.1904; SLM direct effects = -7% per BWN episode, -2.7% per day of mean BWN duration, -18% for any BWN, MWTP = $1,160 per 1-day BWN reduction (Tables 3.8-3.12 truncated after PDF p. 105). Essay 3 (Abstract, PDF p. 4, OLS, N = 110 WV PSDs, DV = residential water charge per 4,500 gallons): multiple raw water sources associated with ~29% higher charges vs single source; NRCS flood-control impoundments NS (Chapter 4 / Table 4.5 truncated after PDF p. 105).
rationale: This 2019 West Virginia University PhD dissertation conducts inferential econometric analyses across three essays, none of which estimates a SWiM-eligible legal/institutional rule-type effect on a Criterion 4 household or community water/sanitation service access outcome: (1) Essay 1 (PDF pp. 17-68, complete with Tables 2.3-2.4) estimates panel and Spatial Durbin models (N = 576, 48 states, 2000-2011) of the share of population served by public water systems incurring SDWA health-based violations on state per capita Personal Health Care expenditures, failing Criterion 4 because the outcome is aggregate medical spending rather than water/sanitation service access. (2) Essay 2 (PDF pp. 70-105) estimates hedonic OLS, spatial lag, and spatial quantile regressions (N = 1,985 single-family sales in Marion County, WV, 2012-2017) of prior-year Boil Water Notices (80% caused by pipe breaks/leaks) on log house sale prices ln(P) and derived marginal willingness to pay (MWTP), failing Criterion 2 (operational unreliability rather than a rule-type legal/tariff/governance intervention) and Criterion 4 (property prices / WTP only). (3) Essay 3 is truncated in the provided prompt text after PDF p. 105 (PDF pp. 106-180 omitted), but the Dissertation Abstract (PDF p. 4), Section 1.1.3 (PDF pp. 12-13), Table of Contents (PDF p. 7), and List of Tables (PDF p. 9) establish that it runs a cross-sectional OLS regression across 110 West Virginia Public Service Districts (Table 4.5) of residential water charges per 4,500 gallons on physical raw water supply source types (surface water, purchased water, multiple sources, NRCS flood-control impoundments) plus utility cost/scope controls (joint water-sewer service, debt, network length) to value raw water; WV Senate Bill 373 is discussed only as statewide policy context rather than a tested exposure. Confidence is set to medium solely because Essay 3's regression table (Table 4.5, p. 165 / PDF p. 174) lies in the truncated tail of the 180-page PDF.

publication_year_note: Printed as Environment and Urbanization Asia, Vol. 4, Issue 1 (2013), pp. 203-220, copyright 2013 National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA); no separate online-first date is printed on the PDF.
rationale: Full text (18 pages) read in full. No inferential hypothesis tests, regression estimates with uncertainty, standard errors, confidence intervals, t/chi-square statistics, or p-values are reported anywhere in the paper. First, the core institutional/governance comparison between centralized metropolitan water provision by the parastatal Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board (BWSSB, N = 1) in Bangalore Metropolitan Center and fragmented municipal provision by 10 Urban Local Bodies (ULBs, N = 10) with KUWS&DB bulk supply in the Bangalore Metropolitan Region (Tables 3-5, PDF pp. 10-13) consists purely of descriptive secondary benchmarking indicators and unweighted arithmetic composite scores (Service Delivery Index: BWSSB = 59.12 vs. 10 ULBs = 21.31 to 52.36; Performance Index: BWSSB = 56.2 vs. 10 ULBs = 13.8 to 47.2), with no statistical test or uncertainty measure. Second, Table 6 (PDF p. 13; discussed p. 14) presents only descriptive 1-decimal-place sample Pearson correlation coefficients (r) across the 11 utilities among the eight MoUD utility service and operational/financial ratios (COV1, COV2, CON, AVI1, AVI2, UNW, OR, RC-Eff.) without any p-values, t-statistics, SEs, or CIs, and none of the eight correlated variables represents a rule-type legal, tenure, governance-structure, ownership, or tariff exposure (UNW, OR, and RC-Eff. are utility water-loss and financial cost-recovery/collection performance ratios). Third, Figure 1 (PDF p. 6) only displays an Excel linear trendline (y = 4.7355x + 1.0387, R2 = 0.4423) on decadal census population growth rates (1881-2011). Flagging quantitative_synthesis_eligible = TRUE is therefore overstated.

publication_year_note: Published in African Journal of Governance and Development, Volume 11, Issue 1.2, November 2022 (pp. 256-275; DOI: 10.36369/2616-9045/2022/v11si2a3); no separate online-first year is printed.
printed_headline_estimate: Chi-square / Cramer's V tests across 6 satisfaction/perception items (n = 448): Gender (Cramer's V = 0.279 to 0.855, P < 0.001, Table 5, PDF p. 10), Age (Cramer's V = 0.262 to 0.688, P < 0.001, Table 6, PDF pp. 11-12), Municipality (Cramer's V = 0.257 to 0.702, P < 0.001, Table 7, PDF p. 14), and Physical Water Source (Cramer's V = 0.357 to 0.801, P < 0.001, Table 8, PDF p. 16).
rationale: The full text reports inferential statistics (Chi-square tests and Cramer's V with P < 0.001 on n = 448 households in Tables 5-8), alongside descriptive statistics on water supply and borehole/tanker functionality (Tables 1-4). However, the tested independent variables are strictly respondent gender (Table 5), respondent age (Table 6), unordered rural municipality name within Vhembe District Municipality (Table 7, Collins Chabane, Makhado, Musina, Thulamela, where variation is attributed to reliance on groundwater vs. piped surface water), and physical water source type (Table 8, borehole, dam tap, river, springs/wells, water tanker). None of the inferential tests evaluates a narrow rule-type legal, tenure, tariff, administrative discretion, enforcement, ownership, or governance exposure against a service access outcome, and 'effectiveness of community participation' is analyzed only as a subjective perception outcome across those four predictors rather than as an explanatory intervention variable. Thus, no SWiM-eligible effect is reported.

publication_year_note: Published in Water Supply Vol 25 No 7, pp. 1125-1141 (© 2025 The Authors; accepted in revised form 5 June 2025; available online 25 June 2025).
rationale: Full text (17 pages) audited. The study applies a descriptive multi-method DPSIR framework combining household questionnaires (154 in 2021 and 259 in 2024; total n = 413), GIS land-use/land-cover percentage changes from MapBiomas, a simple binary cumulative year-over-year growth count (0-7 in Excel) for municipal agricultural, livestock, and industrial indicators, and descriptive comparisons with the ANA Water Security Index (ISH). All reported findings—such as 69.08% of surveyed households experiencing weekly water shortages in 2024, municipal percentages purchasing tanker/barrel water, and proportions of municipalities with consecutive years of cattle or industrial growth—are purely descriptive percentages and counts with zero inferential hypothesis tests, regressions, correlations, standard errors, confidence intervals, or p-values.
